claim: Bovine F1Fo ATP synthase was purified from bovine heart muscle tissue by sucrose density gradient centrifugation and ion-exchange chromatography.
source: Monomeric mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase was purified from bovine heart muscle tissue by sucrose density gradient centrifugation and ion-exchange chromatography.
evidence: The manuscript describes the purification method used in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For 2D crystallisation, fractions with high oligomycin-sensitive ATPase activity (>95%) and high content of native lipids (>100 lipid molecules per F1Fo ATP synthase) were selected.
source: For 2D crystallisation, fractions exhibiting high oligomycin-sensitive ATPase activity (>95%) and a high content of native lipids (>100 lipid molecules per F1Fo ATP synthase) were mixed with synthetic DMPC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the selection criteria for fractions used in crystallization.

claim: When detergent was removed by dialysis, abundant crystalline vesicles formed that were stable for weeks.
source: When the detergent was removed by dialysis, abundant crystalline vesicles formed that were stable for weeks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the formation and stability of crystalline vesicles, with reference to supporting figure.

claim: The crystalline vesicles contained all subunits of the bovine F1Fo ATP synthase, including the small Fo subunits e, f, g, A6L, DAPIT, and the 6.8-kDa protein.
source: Analysis by SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry confirmed that the crystalline vesicles contained all subunits of the bovine F1Fo ATP synthase, including the small Fo subunits e, f, g, A6L, DAPIT, and the 6.8-kDa protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports mass spectrometry and SDS-PAGE analysis confirming subunit composition.

claim: The F1Fo ATP synthase complex in the 2D crystals was intact, active, and highly sensitive to oligomycin (>95%).
source: ATPase assays and blue-native PAGE performed on digitonin-solubilised crystalline vesicles demonstrated that the F1Fo ATP synthase complex in the 2D crystals was intact, active, and highly sensitive to oligomycin (>95%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports ATPase assays and blue-native PAGE results demonstrating enzyme activity and oligomycin sensitivity.

claim: In the tomographic volumes, the F1 subcomplex appears as a 10-nm spherical density attached to the membrane by a thin stalk.
source: In the tomographic volumes, the F1 subcomplex appears as a 10-nm spherical density attached to the membrane by a thin stalk and is arranged in an alternating up-and-down orientation relative to the central lipid bilayer (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from tomographic volumes with reference to figures.

claim: F1 subcomplexes are arranged in an alternating up-and-down orientation relative to the central lipid bilayer.
source: In the tomographic volumes, the F1 subcomplex appears as a 10-nm spherical density attached to the membrane by a thin stalk and is arranged in an alternating up-and-down orientation relative to the central lipid bilayer (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the arrangement of F1 subcomplexes observed in tomographic volumes.

claim: Tomographic cross-sections of crystalline vesicles embedded in thick vitreous ice (>200 nm) showed a zigzag morphology of the membrane.
source: Tomographic cross-sections of crystalline vesicles embedded in thick vitreous ice (>200 nm) showed a zigzag morphology of the membrane (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from tomographic cross-sections with reference to figure.

claim: A total of 2100 F1Fo ATP synthase particles from the flattest regions of rectangular crystalline vesicles were manually selected and averaged by gold standard procedures.
source: A total of 2100 F1Fo ATP synthase particles from the flattest regions of rectangular crystalline vesicles were manually selected and averaged by gold standard procedures (Scheres and Chen, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript describes the particle selection and averaging methodology.

claim: According to the 0.5 FSC criterion, the resulting F1Fo ATP synthase average had a resolution of 24 Å.
source: According to the 0.5 FSC criterion, the resulting F1Fo ATP synthase average had a resolution of 24 Å (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the resolution determined by FSC criterion with reference to figures.

claim: Both the peripheral and central stalks as well as the individual α and β subunits are clearly visible in the subtomogram average.
source: Both the peripheral and central stalks as well as the individual α and β subunits are clearly visible.
evidence: The manuscript describes features visible in the subtomogram average.

claim: The α and β subunits form a non-symmetrical hexamer around the central stalk with alternating long and short sides.
source: The α and β subunits form a non-symmetrical hexamer around the central stalk with alternating long and short sides, allowing an accurate assignment to their respective density regions (Figure 3C,D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural arrangement of α and β subunits observed in the average.

claim: The peripheral stalk is the strongest feature in the sub-tomogram average and is easily visible at contour levels >5σ above the mean.
source: The peripheral stalk is the strongest feature in the sub-tomogram average and is easily visible at contour levels >5σ above the mean.
evidence: The manuscript describes the prominence of the peripheral stalk in the average.

claim: The peripheral stalk of the F1Fo ATP synthase is arranged along the non-catalytic α/β interface and is offset towards the α-subunit.
source: As in other cryo-EM maps (Rubinstein et al., 2003; Lau et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2012), the peripheral stalk of the F1Fo ATP synthase is arranged along the non-catalytic α/β interface and is offset towards the α-subunit, with which it makes contact midway along the stalk (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the position of the peripheral stalk with citations to previous work.

claim: The main contact of the peripheral stalk with the (αβ)3 assembly occurs at the top of the complex.
source: The main contact of the peripheral stalk with the (αβ)3 assembly occurs at the top of the complex (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the contact point between peripheral stalk and catalytic domain.

claim: Two distinct densities are visible at the top of the complex: one above the α-subunit next to the peripheral stalk and the other above the remaining α-subunits.
source: Two distinct densities are visible in this region: one above the α-subunit next to the peripheral stalk and the other above the remaining α-subunits (Figure 3D, d1 and d2, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript describes two distinct densities observed in the structure.

claim: The x-ray structure of the F1/peripheral stalk fragment (PDB: 2WSS) fitted well into the subtomogram average.
source: The first complex we docked into the subtomogram average was the x-ray structure of the F1/peripheral stalk fragment (PDB: 2WSS Rees et al., 2009). All parts of this structure fitted well, with the N-terminal domain of the OSCP occupying the density immediately above the αβα subunits, and the C-terminal domain plus the peripheral stalk occupying the density above the remaining α-subunit.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting of an x-ray structure into the EM density.

claim: The peripheral stalk subcomplex (PDB: 2CLY) did not fit the map when added to the fitted 2WSS structure.
source: The peripheral stalk subcomplex (PDB: 2CLY Dickson et al., 2006) was then added to the fitted 2WSS structure but the resulting structure did not fit the map (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports that a particular structural model did not fit the experimental data.

claim: A modified model combining elements from PDB 2CLY and 2WSS resulted in an excellent match with the EM density.
source: The b-subunit residues 182–207 and the C-terminal domain of the OSCP subunit (residues 115–188) from the 2WSS model were then added to the x-ray structure of the bovine peripheral stalk subcomplex (PDB: 2CLY Dickson et al., 2006) and fitted as a rigid body into the subtomogram average. The new model resulted in an excellent match with the EM density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the creation and fitting of a modified structural model.

claim: The c-ring from the F1/c8 x-ray structure (PDB: 2XND) was fitted by superimposing the F1 subcomplex of this structure with that of 2WSS.
source: Finally the c-ring from the F1/c8 x-ray structure (PDB: 2XND Watt et al., 2010) was fitted by superimposing the F1 subcomplex of this structure with that of 2WSS (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting of the c-ring structure.

claim: The lipid bilayer itself was not resolved in the subtomogram average due to the missing wedge of information in the tomogram.
source: Although the sub-tomogram average was calculated from protein reconstituted into membranes, the lipid bilayer itself was not resolved in the average. This is an effect of the missing wedge of information in the tomogram, which blurs out map features perpendicular to the electron beam, rendering the lipid bilayer in effect invisible (Penczek and Frank, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explains why the lipid bilayer is not visible in the average, citing a technical limitation.

claim: An accurate estimate of the membrane position can be obtained from the position of the c-ring in the fitted atomic model.
source: An accurate estimate of the membrane position can however be obtained from the position of the c-ring in our fitted atomic model (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes how membrane position was estimated from the fitted model.

claim: The subtomogram average was re-inserted into the original tomograms using the inverse of the parameters calculated during averaging.
source: To assess the packing of F1Fo ATP synthases in the 2D crystals, the sub-tomogram average was re-inserted into the original tomograms using the inverse of the parameters calculated during averaging (Pruggnaller et al., 2008; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to analyze crystal packing.

claim: Defects in the 2D crystal lattice were apparent in the rotational orientation of individual complexes in a single layer.
source: Defects in the 2D crystal lattice were apparent in the rotational orientation of individual complexes in a single layer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations of crystal lattice defects.

claim: The F1Fo ATP synthases form pairs of particles of twofold symmetry, which are in contact half-way up the peripheral stalks.
source: The F1Fo ATP synthases form pairs of particles of twofold symmetry, which are in contact half-way up the peripheral stalks.
evidence: The manuscript describes the packing arrangement observed in the crystal.

claim: The angle included by the long axes of the monomers in a pair is approximately 24°.
source: The angle included by the long axes of the monomers in a pair is approximately 24° (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports a measured angle between monomers in a pair.

claim: The ATP synthase pairs in the 2D crystals are structurally unrelated to the native dimers observed in mitochondrial membranes.
source: Note that these ATP synthase pairs in the 2D crystals are structurally unrelated to the native dimers observed in mitochondrial membranes (Strauss et al., 2008; Davies et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the crystal pairs differ from native dimers, citing previous work.

claim: Pairs of F1Fo ATP synthase particles from opposite faces of the lipid bilayer interact via their c-rings and are related to each other by a ∼90° rotation.
source: Pairs of F1Fo ATP synthase particles from opposite faces of the lipid bilayer interact via their c-rings and are related to each other by a ∼90° rotation (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the interaction and orientation of particles across the bilayer.

claim: The pairs of opposing c-rings and the long axes of the F1Fo ATP synthases include an angle of 16° with the crystal plane.
source: In this view, it becomes apparent that the pairs of opposing c-rings and the long axes of the F1Fo ATP synthases include an angle of 16° with the crystal plane.
evidence: The manuscript reports a measured angle of inclination relative to the crystal plane.

claim: In order for the c-rings to be fully embedded in the membrane, the lipid bilayer within the 2D crystals must adopt a zigzag topology.
source: Therefore, in order for the c-rings to be fully embedded in the membrane, the lipid bilayer within the 2D crystals must adopt a zigzag topology, as observed in the vesicle cross-sections (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript infers the zigzag topology from the observed angle and c-ring position.

claim: The bend of the micelle-embedded membrane region of the single-particle map perfectly matched the kink in the membrane required to hold successive c-rings together.
source: To our surprise, the bend of the micelle-embedded membrane region of the single-particle map perfectly matched the kink in the membrane that is required to hold successive c-rings together (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the single-particle map from Baker et al. 2012 matches the observed membrane curvature.

claim: The packing of F1Fo ATP synthases into the 2D crystal strongly supports the notion that the membrane domain of the monomeric bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthases is inherently bent and that this is sufficient to impose a local curvature on the lipid bilayer.
source: Thus the packing of F1Fo ATP synthases into the 2D crystal strongly supports the notion that the membrane domain of the monomeric bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthases is inherently bent and that this is sufficient to impose a local curvature on the lipid bilayer.
evidence: The manuscript draws a conclusion from the observed crystal packing and membrane curvature.

claim: Z-slices through the tomographic volume at the levels of the catalytic (αβ)3 hexamer, the stalk region and the membrane-embedded domain showed sharp diffraction spots to the third order.
source: Z-slices through the tomographic volume at the levels of the catalytic (αβ)3 hexamer, the stalk region and the membrane-embedded domain, which all showed sharp diffraction spots to the third order, were transformed into projection images and processed by electron crystallographic routines without applying symmetry (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2) (Henderson et al., 1986; Crowther et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript describes the quality of diffraction observed in z-slices.

claim: The resulting projection maps were plotted at 30 Å resolution and showed good correlation with the crystal-packing model.
source: The resulting projection maps were plotted at 30 Å resolution and showed good correlation with the crystal-packing model (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports the resolution and quality of correlation between projection maps and model.

claim: For the membrane region, continuous density is observed in the direction of the proposed c-ring/Fo interaction, but not in the perpendicular direction.
source: For the membrane region, where no clear protein density is observed in the subtomogram average, continuous density is observed in the direction of the proposed c-ring/Fo interaction, but not in the perpendicular direction (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript describes the directional density observed in the membrane region.

claim: The zigzag membrane geometry observed in Figure 5C was due to the membrane region of the F1Fo ATP synthase.
source: Thus, the zigzag membrane geometry observed in Figure 5C was due to the membrane region of the F1Fo ATP synthase.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that the membrane region of the enzyme causes the zigzag geometry.

claim: The structure of bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase in the membrane was determined to approximately 24 Å by sub-tomogram averaging of 2D crystals.
source: Sub-tomogram averaging of 2D crystals revealed the structure of bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase in the membrane to approximately 24 Å.
evidence: The manuscript reports the resolution achieved by subtomogram averaging.

claim: A model of molecular packing indicates that the membrane domain of the monomeric F1Fo ATP synthase from bovine heart bends the lipid bilayer.
source: A model of molecular packing, determined by repositioning the sub-tomogram average into the tomographic volume, indicates that the membrane domain of the monomeric F1Fo ATP synthase from bovine heart bends the lipid bilayer.
evidence: The manuscript states the main conclusion about membrane bending by the monomer.

claim: The structure of the bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase reconstituted into a lipid bilayer is consistent with the monomeric detergent-solubilised complex determined by single-particle analysis.
source: Our structure of the bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase reconstituted into a lipid bilayer is consistent with the monomeric detergent-solubilised complex determined by single-particle analysis (Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript compares their structure to a previously published structure.

claim: Several features including the densities of the central and peripheral stalks, the OSCP subunit and the α- and β-subunits are more clearly resolved in the sub-tomogram average than in the single-particle map at 18 Å.
source: Even though the resolution of our sub-tomogram average at 24 Å is nominally less good than that of the single-particle map at 18 Å, several features are more clearly resolved. This includes the densities of the central and peripheral stalks, the OSCP subunit and the α- and β-subunits, which are clearly separated in the sub-tomogram average (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript compares the clarity of features in their map versus a previous map.

claim: The improved clarity of features may be a result of more accurate particle alignment using 3D volumes rather than 2D projection images.
source: This may be a result of the more accurate particle alignment, which used 3D volumes rather than 2D projection images.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for the improved clarity of features.

claim: The resolution of the sub-tomogram average is about 1.5× better in the x–y plane than the z direction due to the single orientation of F1Fo ATP synthase particles in the crystal relative to the missing wedge of information.
source: The resolution of our sub-tomogram average is about 1.5× better in the x–y plane than the z direction due to the single orientation of F1Fo ATP synthase particles in the crystal relative to the missing wedge of information (Radermacher, 1988).
evidence: The manuscript explains the anisotropic resolution with citation to previous work.

claim: In the sub-tomogram average, the peripheral stalk is positioned along the non-catalytic αβ interface but is more offset towards the α-subunit than in the x-ray structure.
source: In our sub-tomogram average, the peripheral stalk is positioned along the non-catalytic αβ interface as previously reported (Rees et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2012) but is more offset towards the α-subunit than in the x-ray structure (Rees et al., 2009; Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript compares the position of the peripheral stalk in their structure to previous structures.

claim: A small connecting density is visible between the midpoint of the peripheral stalk and α-subunit.
source: A small connecting density visible between the midpoint of the peripheral stalk and α-subunit may account for this difference.
evidence: The manuscript describes an observed density feature.

claim: A similar connection between peripheral stalk and α-subunit is seen in the single-particle cryo-EM map of the bovine complex.
source: A similar connection is seen in the single-particle cryo-EM map of the bovine complex (Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript notes a similar feature in a previously published structure.

claim: Analysis of the fitted x-ray structure suggests possible ionic interactions between subunit d and residues 463–475 of the α-subunit.
source: Analysis of the fitted x-ray structure suggests possible ionic interactions between subunit d and residues 463–475 of the α-subunit, which is the point where the structures of the α and β-subunits diverge (Walker et al., 1982).
evidence: The manuscript proposes possible interactions based on analysis of the fitted structure.

claim: The additional contact between peripheral stalk and α-subunit may help the peripheral stalk in its role as a stator.
source: This additional contact may help the peripheral stalk in its role as a stator, but may also prevent the stalk from interfering with the catalytic cycle of the β-subunit by pulling it away from the α/β interface.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the functional significance of the observed contact.

claim: The dominant density of the peripheral stalk in the sub-tomogram average suggests that this region is more rigid than other parts of the complex.
source: The dominant density of the peripheral stalk in the sub-tomogram average suggests that this region is more rigid than other parts of the complex.
evidence: The manuscript infers rigidity from the strength of the density.

claim: The bovine heart peripheral stalk fragment extended by several residues from the F1-peripheral stalk structure was fitted into the density as a rigid body without the need to introduce hinges.
source: In accordance with this, we were able to fit the bovine heart peripheral stalk fragment (Dickson et al., 2006) extended by several residues from the F1-peripheral stalk structure (Rees et al., 2009) into the density as a rigid body without the need to introduce hinges as previously suggested (Baker et al., 2012) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting of a structural model and compares to previous suggestions.

claim: The rigid body fit of the peripheral stalk challenges the notion that the peripheral stalk acts as a flexible linker that stores torque or elastic energy during the catalytic cycle.
source: This fit therefore challenges the notion that the peripheral stalk acts as a flexible linker that stores torque or elastic energy during the catalytic cycle (Sorgen et al., 1998; Sorgen et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript states that their findings challenge a previous hypothesis, citing the relevant work.

claim: The hypothesis that the peripheral stalk acts as a flexible linker was based on the bacterial enzyme, which has a peripheral stalk consisting of only two long alpha helices.
source: This hypothesis was based on the bacterial enzyme, which has a peripheral stalk consisting of only two long alpha helices.
evidence: The manuscript provides context for the previous hypothesis.

claim: The bovine peripheral stalk consists of one long alpha helix plus subunits d, F6 and the N-terminal domains of other Fo subunits, which would generate a more rigid structure.
source: The bovine peripheral stalk, in contrast, consists of one long alpha helix plus subunits d, F6 and the N-terminal domains of other Fo subunits, which would generate a more rigid structure (Dickson et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the bovine peripheral stalk and infers its rigidity.

claim: A rigid peripheral stalk would hold the (αβ)3 hexamer in a stationary position relative to the membrane.
source: A rigid peripheral stalk would hold the (αβ)3 hexamer in a stationary position relative to the membrane.
evidence: The manuscript infers a functional consequence of peripheral stalk rigidity.

claim: A rigid peripheral stalk is probably more important in mitochondria than in bacteria because the mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase has another important role in generating local membrane curvature and maintaining cristae morphology through the formation of dimer rows.
source: This is probably more important in mitochondria than in bacteria, as the mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase has another important role in generating local membrane curvature and maintaining cristae morphology through the formation of dimer rows (Davies et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the functional importance of peripheral stalk rigidity in mitochondria, citing previous work.

claim: The dimer interface is located at the base of the peripheral stalk.
source: The dimer interface is located at the base of the peripheral stalk (Davies et al., 2011, 2012) and thus any flexibility in the structure of the peripheral stalk may compromise the formation and stability of the dimer.
evidence: The manuscript states the location of the dimer interface, citing previous work.

claim: Any flexibility in the structure of the peripheral stalk may compromise the formation and stability of the dimer.
source: The dimer interface is located at the base of the peripheral stalk (Davies et al., 2011, 2012) and thus any flexibility in the structure of the peripheral stalk may compromise the formation and stability of the dimer.
evidence: The manuscript speculates on the consequences of peripheral stalk flexibility for dimer formation.

claim: The membrane-embedded parts in the sub-tomogram average were not well-resolved.
source: Despite the prominent structural features visible in the membrane-extrinsic regions of the F1Fo ATP synthase, the membrane-embedded parts in our sub-tomogram average were not well-resolved (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the lack of resolution in the membrane-embedded region.

claim: The c-ring, located directly beneath the central stalk, is easily visible in x-ray models filtered to 20 Å resolution.
source: This was surprising as the c-ring, located directly beneath the central stalk, is easily visible in x-ray models filtered to 20 Å resolution.
evidence: The manuscript notes that the c-ring should be visible at the achieved resolution based on filtered x-ray models.

claim: Only a weak density for the c-ring is seen in the sub-tomogram average.
source: In our sub-tomogram average, we only see a weak density for the c-ring.
evidence: The manuscript reports the weak density observed for the c-ring.

claim: The lack of detail in the membrane region is unlikely to be caused by the missing wedge.
source: The lack of detail in the membrane region is unlikely to be caused by the missing wedge as we have observed a similar phenomenon in sub-tomogram averages of other membrane proteins, which have no missing wedge of information, and in single-particle maps when the resolution does not extend beyond 15 Å.
evidence: The manuscript argues against the missing wedge as the cause based on observations of other proteins.

claim: The lack of protein density in the membrane region at this resolution seems to be caused mainly by contrast matching between the surrounding lipid and protein.
source: Thus, the lack of protein density in the membrane region for our averages at this resolution seems to be caused mainly by contrast matching between the surrounding lipid and protein.
evidence: The manuscript proposes contrast matching as the explanation for lack of membrane region density.

claim: The projection images generated from selected z-slices of tomographic volumes enabled the use of electron crystallographic image processing, even though the coherently packed areas of the 2D crystals were small.
source: The projection images generated from selected z-slices of tomographic volumes enabled us to use electron crystallographic image processing, even though the coherently packed areas of the 2D crystals were small.
evidence: The manuscript describes the advantage of their approach for processing small crystals.

claim: The approach improved the signal-to-noise ratio because noise originating from additional crystal layers or surrounding buffer was removed in silico by careful selection of the z-slices and Fourier filtering of the diffraction pattern.
source: This improved the signal-to-noise ratio because noise originating from additional crystal layers or surrounding buffer was removed in silico by careful selection of the z-slices and Fourier filtering of the diffraction pattern.
evidence: The manuscript explains how their approach improves signal-to-noise ratio.

claim: 2D processing of tomographic 3D crystal volumes poses an attractive alternative for the electron crystallographic treatment of small 2D crystals of large membrane complexes that are not accessible to canonical image processing due to limited size and order.
source: Thus 2D processing of tomographic 3D crystal volumes poses an attractive alternative for the electron crystallographic treatment of small 2D crystals of large membrane complexes that are not accessible to canonical image processing due to limited size and order.
evidence: The manuscript proposes their approach as a general method for small crystals.

claim: The molecular packing of multi-subunit membrane complexes with large extramembranous domains can be complicated with multiple layers and multiple tilt angles relative to the crystal plane.
source: As exemplified in our 2D crystal of the F1Fo ATP synthase, the molecular packing of multi-subunit membrane complexes with large extramembranous domains can be complicated with multiple layers and multiple tilt angles relative to the crystal plane.
evidence: The manuscript generalizes from their observations about complex packing.

claim: The approach of combining electron tomography with electron crystallography enables a straightforward interpretation of projection maps in cases of complicated molecular packing.
source: These are circumstances under which projection maps alone are easily misinterpreted and our approach of combining electron tomography with electron crystallography enables a straightforward interpretation (Gerle et al., 2006; Tani et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript argues for the advantage of their combined approach, citing previous work.

claim: In mitochondria, the F1Fo ATP synthase forms rows of dimers along the highly curved ridges of cristae membranes.
source: In mitochondria, the F1Fo ATP synthase forms rows of dimers along the highly curved ridges of cristae membranes (Strauss et al., 2008; Davies et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states a known fact about ATP synthase organization in mitochondria, citing previous work.

claim: Disruption of dimers prevents the formation of wild-type cristae and increases the generation time of the organism.
source: Disruption of dimers prevents the formation of wild-type cristae and increases the generation time of the organism (Paumard et al., 2002; Davies et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work showing the consequences of disrupting dimers.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that the F1Fo ATP synthase dimer structure alone is sufficient to bend the lipid bilayer and drive row formation.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that the F1Fo ATP synthase dimer structure alone is sufficient to bend the lipid bilayer and drive row formation (Davies et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous simulation work on membrane bending by dimers.

claim: Single-particle cryo-EM of mitochondrial ATP synthase complexes indicates that the bend of the dimer may originate from the structure of the Fo domain in a single monomer.
source: In addition, single-particle cryo-EM of mitochondrial ATP synthase complexes indicates that the bend of the dimer may originate from the structure of the Fo domain in a single monomer (Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work suggesting that the monomer may be bent.

claim: Analysis of the F1Fo ATP synthase packing in 2D crystals showed that the Fo domain of monomeric bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase induces a substantial kink in the lipid bilayer.
source: Through our analysis of the F1Fo ATP synthase packing in 2D crystals, we have shown that the Fo domain of monomeric bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase indeed induces a substantial kink in the lipid bilayer (Figures 5, 6) explaining in molecular terms the zigzag appearance of the membrane in the 2D crystals (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript states their main finding about membrane bending by the monomer.

claim: When two monomeric complexes join to form a dimer in the inner mitochondrial membrane, the resulting angle between the long axes of the monomers would be ∼86°.
source: When two monomeric complexes join to form a dimer in the inner mitochondrial membrane, the resulting angle between the long axes of the monomers would be ∼86° (Figure 7) exactly as observed in the subtomogram averages of the bovine F1Fo ATP synthase dimer (Davies et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript predicts the dimer angle based on monomer geometry and compares to previous observations.

claim: The dimer angle of ∼86° gives rise to the high local curvature of membranes required to shape the cristae.
source: This dimer angle gives rise to the high local curvature of membranes required to shape the cristae (Davies et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript connects the dimer angle to cristae morphology, citing previous work.

claim: The F1Fo monomer is the basic building block of the ATP synthase dimer rows.
source: We conclude that the F1Fo monomer is the basic building block of the ATP synthase dimer rows.
evidence: The manuscript states their conclusion about the role of the monomer.

claim: Newly assembled monomeric complexes of the bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase would converge on pre-existing regions of high membrane curvature where they assemble into dimers, thus propagating the self-association of dimers into rows.
source: Newly assembled monomeric complexes of the bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase monomers would converge on pre-existing regions of high membrane curvature where they assemble into dimers, thus propagating the self-association of dimers into rows.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a model for how monomers assemble into dimer rows.

claim: The bovine heart enzyme has a molecular mass of approximately 600 kDa.
source: The bovine heart enzyme has a molecular mass of approximately 600 kDa and consists of 17 different subunits (α3, β3, γ, δ, ε, a, b, c8, d, e, f, g, A6L, F6, oligomycin sensitivity conferral protein [OSCP], DAPIT, and a 6.8 kDa protein) (Meyer et al., 2007; Runswick et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states the molecular mass of the enzyme, citing previous work.

claim: The bovine heart F1Fo ATP synthase consists of 17 different subunits.
source: The bovine heart enzyme has a molecular mass of approximately 600 kDa and consists of 17 different subunits (α3, β3, γ, δ, ε, a, b, c8, d, e, f, g, A6L, F6, oligomycin sensitivity conferral protein [OSCP], DAPIT, and a 6.8 kDa protein) (Meyer et al., 2007; Runswick et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript lists the subunit composition, citing previous work.

claim: The enzyme can be subdivided into four essential functional parts: the catalytic part (αβ)3, the membrane-embedded part, the central stalk γδε, and the peripheral stalk.
source: The enzyme can be subdivided into four essential functional parts: the catalytic part, (αβ)3, which binds and converts ADP and Pi to ATP; the membrane-embedded part (a, b, c8, e, f, g, A6L, DAPIT, and the 6.8 kDa protein) through which protons move across the membrane; the central stalk, γδε, which transmits the rotation of the membrane-embedded rotor-ring (c8) to the catalytic region; and the peripheral stalk (b, d, F6 and OSCP) which holds the catalytic part stationary relative to the membrane region.
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional organization of the enzyme.

claim: The catalytic part (αβ)3 binds and converts ADP and Pi to ATP.
source: The enzyme can be subdivided into four essential functional parts: the catalytic part, (αβ)3, which binds and converts ADP and Pi to ATP
evidence: The manuscript describes the function of the catalytic domain.

claim: The membrane-embedded part consists of subunits a, b, c8, e, f, g, A6L, DAPIT, and the 6.8 kDa protein, through which protons move across the membrane.
source: the membrane-embedded part (a, b, c8, e, f, g, A6L, DAPIT, and the 6.8 kDa protein) through which protons move across the membrane
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition and function of the membrane-embedded part.

claim: The central stalk γδε transmits the rotation of the membrane-embedded rotor-ring (c8) to the catalytic region.
